Description: Enforce strict validation on all API inputs to prevent injection attacks and invalid parameters. Validate strictly against the MCP schema and reject malformed, oversized, or out-of-specification requests.
Implement per-user, per-agent, and per-session rate limits on tool invocations to prevent abuse or DoS attacks. Set timeouts and throttling for costly operations.
Properly encode and sanitize API outputs before surfacing to model context. Strip markup and validate structured fields to prevent format-embedded poisoning.

Implement role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC), limit resource access, and enforce the principle of least privilege. Use policy engines such as Open Policy Agent or Cedar.

Securely manage and store service credentials; avoid hard-coded secrets and use key management services. Adopt a secret-broker pattern — tools obtain short-lived credentials from a vault at call time. Rotate automatically.
Use secure methods when authenticating with third-party services. Enforce OAuth 2.1 with audience-bound scoped tokens; forbid token passthrough to downstream APIs.
Run service processes with the minimum required permissions. Issue narrowly scoped OAuth tokens per tool invocation; tokens should expire after the task completes.
Automatically rotate API keys and service credentials periodically, limiting the valid timeframe. Segment across distinct wallets or accounts with spending limits for high-risk tools.
Provide a mechanism for clients to verify the server's identity using PKI or cryptographic attestation. Enforce TLS certificates; reject self-signed or mismatched identities; implement mutual TLS.
Implement strict lifecycle management for MCP plugins and coordinate with the client. Ensure graceful termination, token invalidation, and resource cleanup at shutdown.
Forcefully clean up all MCP background processes, active sessions, access tokens, and API keys when the client shuts down. Invalidate all credentials to prevent orphaned session abuse.
Regularly check the status of MCP plugins to detect abnormal persistence, stale connections, or configuration drift.
Monitor and log all MCP background activities, tool invocations, and context updates using structured telemetry sent to a SIEM.
Limit the operations and duration that MCP plugins can perform in the background. Enforce quotas and rate limits to prevent resource exhaustion.

Server runs in an isolated environment (container, VM, or sandbox) to prevent escape and mitigate lateral movement. Run as non-root; mount root filesystem read-only; apply seccomp and AppArmor profiles.
Adopt hardened container security configurations and run containers as non-root users. Employ immutable infrastructure, runtime protection, signed images, and Kubernetes Pod Security Standards.
Validate service boot processes implementing secure boot chains and integrity checks. Verify image signatures via Cosign/Sigstore before deployment.
Protect sensitive environment variables and ensure they are not exposed in logs, traces, or model context. Use a secret broker pattern; pass only opaque handles to tools.
Enforce CPU, memory, and network resource usage limits per container and per tool to prevent DoS and resource exhaustion. Apply quotas via Kubernetes LimitRange/ResourceQuota.
Use digital signatures, cryptographic hash checks (SHA-256+), and SLSA-conformant provenance attestations to ensure code has not been tampered with. Verify signatures at install and update time.
Support mechanisms for remote verification of code integrity using Sigstore/Cosign or equivalent transparency logs. Reject unsigned or hash-mismatched artifacts at admission.
Apply code obfuscation and hardening techniques to increase the difficulty of reverse engineering. Use SAST and software composition analysis in CI/CD pipelines.
Securely manage third-party dependencies. Run software composition analysis (SCA) and SAST in CI. Pin dependency versions and verify hashes. Monitor for known CVEs in transitive dependencies.
Verify the integrity and authenticity of packages using cryptographic hash checks and signed package manifests before install. Block packages from unverified sources.
Validate the source of all code and dependencies against a curated, organization-approved registry. Only allow tools from allow-listed origins with stable identifiers such as image digests.
Ensure the build process is secure using hardened CI/CD pipelines with SLSA supply-chain integrity objectives, signed artifacts, and build provenance attestation.
Detect and report anomalous activity patterns using behavioral baselines over per-tool call frequency, prompt length, response size, and tool-chain fan-out. Alert on deviations.
Log all service activities and security events including authentication attempts, tool invocations, configuration edits, and policy decisions as structured, immutable audit records.
Configure real-time alerts for critical security events: auth failures, policy denials, WAF/HIDS hits, sandbox escapes, and exfiltration indicators (unusual egress volume or destination).
Collect and analyze logs from all MCP components in a centralized SIEM (e.g. Splunk or Elastic) to reconstruct incident timelines across hosts, clients, and servers.
Ensure log integrity using append-only/WORM storage, chained hashing of records, and periodic anchoring to an external trusted timestamping service to prevent tampering.
Provide detailed auditing and incident investigation capabilities including distributed tracing that correlates edge-to-server-to-tool for each request. Retain logs aligned with regulatory minima.
Ensure operational isolation among multiple MCP Servers using dedicated pods with separate service accounts, network policies, and minimal RBAC footprints.
Assign each MCP Server a clearly defined resource access boundary enforced via Kubernetes NetworkPolicies and fine-grained RBAC. Restrict to approved MCP servers and internal control endpoints only.
Use distinct, narrowly scoped permission sets for tools in different domains. Each tool invocation should mint its own audience-limited, scope-limited OAuth token.
Implement suitable resource isolation strategies according to different operating system characteristics including seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux, and no_new_privs flags.
Test consistent security behavior of MCP Server across different OS and clients, including verifying that security controls are not bypassed by platform-specific edge cases.
Evaluate unique security risks specific to each platform and apply mitigating measures. Conduct red-team exercises and include MCP-specific attack scenarios in test suites.
Ensure security controls can adapt to differences among various client implementations. Validate behavior across Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, and other MCP-aware clients.
Collect and process only the necessary data. Apply emergent aggregation risk controls — limit cross-tool context accumulation that could reveal sensitive patterns no single call would expose.
Encrypt sensitive data in storage (AES-256) and transit (TLS 1.2+). Enforce mutual TLS for service-to-service MCP communications inside clusters.
Ensure effective isolation of different users' and tenants' data. Enforce session boundaries to prevent cross-tenant context leakage in shared MCP server deployments.
Enforce strict access controls on data using RBAC/ABAC. Prevent cross-tool data flows that redirect internal content to external endpoints without explicit authorization.
Automatically identify and handle sensitive data including PII, credentials, and proprietary content. Scrub or tokenize before logs are aggregated. Apply DLP scanning on model responses.

Implement fine-grained access control for resources using scoped OAuth tokens per resource type. Validate audience and scope on every request; reject calls that exceed the policy attached to the resource.
Limit the size and quantity of a single resource. Enforce rate limits per user, agent, or session to prevent resource exhaustion and DoS.
Validate and sanitize template parameters of resources. Treat resource templates as untrusted input; enforce strict schemas and character allow-lists.
Label and handle sensitive resources distinctly. Apply tiered sensitivity classification and enforce stronger authorization gates for high-sensitivity resource access.
Adhere to security coding standards and best practices including OWASP guidelines, input validation cheat sheets, and MCP-specific hardening guidance.
Execute tools in a controlled environment to prevent system-level impact. Use per-tool containers with read-only root filesystems, non-root execution, and default-deny egress.
Strictly validate all inputs from clients against defined schemas before tool execution. Reject malformed, oversized, or policy-violating parameters at the gateway layer.
Each tool should have only the minimum permissions needed to complete its task. Mint scoped, short-lived OAuth tokens per invocation; enforce audience and scope at the server before execution.
Validate the data processed by tools to prevent injection or tampering. Do not insert returned third-party data directly into model context without sanitization.
Restrict the range and types of actions a tool can perform using allow-lists of permitted operations, domains, and file paths. Enforce directory allow-lists at creation time.

Verify that returned information from third-party interfaces matches expected schemas. Do not directly insert returned data into model context; sanitize and validate first to prevent format-embedded poisoning.
Handle errors securely without exposing sensitive information such as stack traces, internal URLs, or credentials in error responses visible to the model or end user.
Enforce strict namespace isolation for different tools to prevent command and function collisions. Use unique identifiers or namespaces to prevent one server's tools from shadowing another's.
The UI should clearly display the scope of AI operations and potential impacts, offering an intuitive security indicator and consent mechanism for tool invocations.

High-risk operations (e.g. file deletion, fund transfers, irreversible actions) must explicitly require user confirmation. Present structured context showing data read/write scope and external contacts.
Permission requests should explicitly state their purpose and scope so users can make informed decisions and avoid over-authorization. Highlight scope mismatches and escalate to a higher trust tier.
Tool invocation and data access should be visible and auditable by users, accompanied by detailed operation logs and distributed tracing correlated across host, client, and server.
Tools should allow users to choose whether to display hidden tags by default (such as <SECRET>) to prevent malicious logic embedding and ANSI escape code injection.
Users should be able to clearly understand the current MCP operations in progress, including which tools are active and what data is being accessed.
Record all critical AI operations and their results using structured, immutable audit logs. Correlate tool invocations with identity claims, token status, and policy decisions.
Detect abnormal patterns of tool invocation or request sequences using behavioral baselines. Flag sudden spikes in tool usage, unusually long prompts, or unexpected fan-out across servers.
Impose frequency and quantity limits on tool calls per user, agent, and session. Block runaway workflows that could exhaust resources or trigger denial of service.
Use a system keychain or dedicated encrypted storage for sensitive credentials to prevent unauthorized access. Apply a secret-broker pattern so tools receive ephemeral vault-issued credentials.
Implement mechanisms to isolate sensitive user data from ordinary data in storage and processing. Sanitize residual data in logs, caches, and crash dumps after session ends.
Validate the integrity of the application and MCP plugins to prevent tampering. Verify digital signatures via Cosign/Sigstore at install and update time; fail closed on signature mismatch.
Verify the digital signatures of Host application updates and MCP tool definitions. Treat any change to a tool definition as untrusted until re-validated; require fresh approval workflows.
Whenever possible, run the application in a sandbox environment to limit system access. Apply gVisor or equivalent sandboxing runtimes for untrusted tool execution.
Enforce authentication before communicating with any critical MCP Server, preventing anonymous access. Implement per-request identity verification rather than relying on session-level trust.

Correctly implement OAuth 2.1 or higher, following best practices. Enforce audience-bound tokens; validate issuer, audience, scope, and expiration on every request; deny expired or wrong-audience tokens.
For web clients, use a state parameter to mitigate CSRF attacks, employing a unique random value for each authorization request.
Validate the authenticity and integrity of registered tools by verifying cryptographic signatures and hashes before admission. Reject unknown tool IDs or hash-mismatched definitions.
The MCP client should regularly check for and apply security updates. Treat any post-approval tool definition change as untrusted — require re-validation to detect rug-pull style redefinitions.
Check for name conflicts or malicious overwriting before registering any tool. Use namespaces or unique identifiers to prevent cross-server tool shadowing and command collisions.
Monitor and identify potentially malicious MCP behavior including poisoned tool metadata, hidden instructions in descriptions, ANSI escape code injection, and preference manipulation.
Use namespaces or unique identifiers to avoid naming collisions. Enforce a curated allow-list of approved tool names and origins; reject discovery of tools outside the list.
Maintain an authorized registry of trustworthy MCP Servers and tools with recorded versions, hashes, and cryptographic signatures stored in tamper-evident transparency logs.
Establish clear rules to resolve tool name conflicts using explicit priority rules and provenance verification. Document and enforce disambiguation policies across all MCP hosts.
Isolate tools in different domains to prevent cross-impact. Use dedicated containers and network policies per tool domain to contain blast radius.
Set explicit tool priority rules to avoid malicious overwriting. Bind to specific signed versions rather than whatever happens to be served under a name at invocation time.
Version functions and tools to detect changes. Use immutable, cryptographically signed tool definitions — any change in behavior requires a new version and renewed approval.

Define clear processes for tool registration and de-registration to prevent leftover tools posing security risks. Treat the server tool list as the single source of truth and actively remove stale entries.
Detect and resolve function and resource conflicts in multi-MCP environments including cross-origin tool shadowing and slash-command overlap.
Classify tools according to sensitivity and risk level. Apply risk-aware differentiation — route high-sensitivity tool calls through stronger authorization gates and just-in-time access controls.
Implement layered defense measures to prevent prompt injection attacks including gateway-level payload blocking, output sanitization, and manual verification for critical executions.
Detect and block potential malicious instructions embedded in tool descriptions, prompt templates, retrieved documents, or third-party API responses before surfacing to the model.
Clearly separate system prompts from user inputs to prevent tampering. Enforce strict schemas and sanitization on tool metadata and prompts before exposure to the model.
Filter out sensitive personal data, credentials, and PII from prompts and context using DLP controls. Scrub or tokenize before logs are aggregated.
Ensure that contexts from different sources remain isolated to prevent contamination or information leakage. Separate retrieval-based content from trusted system instructions.
Use secure prompt templates from vetted servers only. Treat server-supplied templates as untrusted input; validate before injecting into the model context.
Check tool descriptions for potential malicious instructions, hidden directives, ANSI escape sequences, and preference manipulation phrasing before surfacing during discovery.
Ensure that identical prompts produce predictable and consistent results across different environments. Include adversarial prompt test cases in security benchmarks.
Clearly define the mechanism for cleaning up historical context to prevent data buildup and leakage. Apply explicit session teardown and context purge policies.

Record all interactions with the MCP Server, tool calls, and authorization activities as structured traces capturing principal identity, token status, targeted server/tool, method, latency, and outcome.
Log all security-related events including authorization failures, policy denials, and anomalous tool call sequences. Route to immutable, tamper-evident centralized storage.
Detect and alert on abnormal activity patterns including consent fatigue signals, unusual prompt sizes, unexpected tool chains, and egress to newly observed domains.
Verify the identity of the MCP Server before connecting. Implement certificate pinning or PKI-based verification. Reject connections to servers with self-signed or mismatched certificates.
Strictly validate TLS certificates of remote Servers to prevent Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. Enforce strong cipher suites; disable TLS 1.0/1.1; reject expired or invalid certificates.
Use TLS 1.2+ to encrypt all Client-Server communications; disable weak cipher suites. Apply mutual TLS for service-to-service MCP traffic inside clusters using a service mesh.
Configure secure TLS parameters, regularly review and update encryption algorithms. Enforce default-deny egress with explicit allow-lists of permitted destinations.
Strictly limit the scope of tokens under the principle of least privilege. Mint audience-bound, service-specific, short-lived tokens per tool invocation; forbid passthrough to third-party APIs.
Carefully control which tools and operations can be auto-approved. Pause automatic use when a tool is first encountered or a new version is detected; require fresh approval.
Maintain an explicit whitelist of tools and operations that can be auto-approved, pinned by registry origin, image digest, or UUID. Reject discovery of tools outside the allow-list.
Dynamically adjust auto-approve policies based on runtime context, time-of-day, data sensitivity, and recent anomaly signals. Apply context-aware revalidation when conditions change.
Log and audit all auto-approval decisions including the tool identity, scope granted, approving principal, and timestamp. Flag scope-expansion attempts versus baseline.
Strictly control the scope of context included in sampling requests. Do not aggregate cross-tool outputs into shared model context beyond what is necessary for the task.
Filter out sensitive data from sampling requests and responses before surfacing to the model context or external endpoints.
Validate all parameters and content within sampling requests. Treat server-initiated sampling as untrusted input subject to the same injection defenses as user prompts.
Ensure users have clear control over sampling requests and results including the ability to review, reject, or pause model-initiated tool calls.
Handle model preference information securely to prevent preference manipulation attacks where biased tool descriptions steer the model toward unsafe or attacker-controlled tools.
Verify that sampling results conform to security standards and do not contain malicious instructions, exfiltration payloads, or format-embedded poisoning artifacts.
Ensure the LLM can correctly prioritize and execute the intended plugin functions. Apply allow-lists and signed tool definitions to prevent malicious tools from being preferred over legitimate ones.

The LLM should identify and defend against malicious mnemonic or injection instructions within prompts, tool descriptions, and retrieved content. Apply guardrails and Constitutional AI-style self-critique.
The LLM should securely and correctly invoke relevant MCP functionalities. Validate tool call parameters before execution; enforce intent-aware authorization checks at runtime.
Prevent leakage of sensitive information through model outputs, sampling responses, or tool call parameters. Apply DLP scanning and output sanitization before results are surfaced.

Filter out harmful or sensitive information in multi-modal content (e.g. malicious prompt text within images or PDFs). Treat retrieved multi-modal content as untrusted before injecting into model context.
Ensure overall security in multi-MCP environments; periodically scan and inspect installed MCPs for poisoned metadata, stale manifests, and misconfigured permissions.
Check for potential malicious prompt presets to prevent hijacking of function priority. Verify tool descriptions and metadata for hidden directives before registration.
Implement secure control over cross-MCP function calls to prevent malicious cascade actions. Enforce per-agent scoped tokens; validate audience on every handoff to prevent confused-deputy escalation.
When one agent or MCP server delegates to another, enforce identity verification and token audience binding. Forbid token passthrough; require fresh scoped credentials on each handoff.
Monitor inter-agent message patterns for signs of coordinated policy bypass or covert communication. Apply cross-agent behavioral correlation in the SIEM to surface colluding workflows.
Guard multi-agent workflows against accumulated shadow logic and re-enabled deprecated behaviors using policy engines, tool-list change notifications, and periodic orchestration audits.
Enforce verified namespaces and PKI-based server identity to prevent typosquatting and look-alike endpoint registration. Require cryptographic proof of identity before client binding.
Mandate mutual TLS for all MCP client-server communications in production. Validate client certificates; reject connections lacking strong client identity; monitor TLS handshake failures.
Remove all implicit trust assumptions in MCP deployments. Treat every tool invocation as a fresh authorization decision; verify identity, audience, scope, and expiration on each request.

Harden container runtimes to prevent sandbox escapes. Apply gVisor, seccomp deny-by-default profiles, and AppArmor/SELinux policies. Monitor for privilege escalation attempts via Falco or eBPF sensors.
Prohibit root or Administrator execution for MCP tools and helper processes. Enforce runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, and drop all non-required Linux capabilities.
Isolate MCP instances to prevent lateral movement via shared infrastructure. Segment network access; use per-server credential wallets; prohibit shared token stores across server boundaries.
Apply output perturbation, differential privacy techniques, and query rate limiting to mitigate model inversion and membership inference attacks against shared enterprise LLM backends.
Validate training and fine-tuning pipelines for backdoor injection risks. Apply data provenance checks and adversarial robustness evaluation before deploying models into MCP agent workflows.
Maintain an inventory of all MCP servers in the organization. Periodically scan GitHub and internal registries for unauthorized or ungoverned MCP deployments that bypass central security review.

Establish an organizational MCP Server Marketplace or registry requiring security review, automated scanning, and signing before approval. Apply SOC 2 or equivalent certification for high-risk connectors.
